bkn: A single-binary backend core: document collections, typed settings, identity, file storage, an event log, scheduled jobs, and sandboxed scripts over embedded SQLite, driven entirely from the CLI.
one_liner: bkn gives a project the two primitives every backend re-invents - a place to put documents and a place to put settings - as one static binary with no database server, no runtime, and no admin UI. Every capability is a CLI verb first and an HTTP route second.

model.single binary: The tool is the server, the client and the migration runner. There is nothing else to install and no container to build.
model.single writer: bkn owns its SQLite file. Consumers reach it through the CLI or the HTTP API, never by opening the database themselves. This is the rule that keeps the data model changeable.
model.two primitives: store holds documents; kv holds typed settings; auth holds users, organizations and tokens; files holds blobs; events is the append-only log; cron schedules scripts; script runs sandboxed JavaScript over all of them. Features are built on top of these, not added beside them.
model.namespaces: Every collection is addressed as <namespace>/<collection>. The namespace is the owning app, so two apps never collide and no caller has to guess a table name.
model.cli is the api: Any verb available over HTTP is available as a subcommand with the same shape. Agents drive the CLI; browsers and services drive the HTTP routes.
model.scripts are userland: Anything that is a scheduled HTTP call, a transform over stored records, or a webhook handler is a script, not a core feature. This is what keeps the core small enough to change.
model.identity is not billing: auth carries no subscription, plan or Stripe fields. In the system bkn replaces they lived on the user record, and the missing endpoint to write one is what drove a consumer to bypass the API and write the database directly. Billing belongs in a store collection, managed by a script.
model.errors, audit and metrics are one thing: They differ only in which field you care about. An event has a stream, a type, a level, a subject and a JSON body; three separate admin domains collapse into one primitive.
model.inbound events: hooks is the inbound counterpart to bkn.http.fetch. A public URL delivers a third-party event to a script, which verifies the sender's signature itself with bkn.crypto. Without it no signed integration could ever be userland.
model.lifecycle: bkn keeps itself current and reports on itself: `update` swaps in a newer binary after verifying and running it, `install` puts a binary already in hand onto PATH, `feedback` reaches the operator, and `telemetry` counts verbs - opt-in, because this tool holds secrets.

loop: bkn guide - read this, once, to learn the model
bkn help-json - discover the exact commands, flags and exit codes
bkn store put myapp/users --data '{"email":"A@B.io"}' - write a document; the collection is created on first write
bkn store find myapp/users --where email=a@b.io - read it back by any field
bkn kv set myapp.stripe_key sk_live_... --type encrypted - store a secret sealed with the active key
bkn script test --file draft.js --input '{}' - try a script before storing it
bkn script create digest --file draft.js - store it, then run it by name or over HTTP
bkn files put assets ./logo.png - store a blob; bkn files get assets logo.png reads it back
bkn serve - expose the same primitives over HTTP when a service needs them
bkn daemon start - background that server and poll it healthy
bkn cron create nightly --schedule '@daily' --script digest - run a script on a schedule
bkn events list errors --since 24h --level error - see what broke

concepts.ref: A collection address, '<namespace>/<collection>'. Both segments are lowercase, start with a letter, and may contain digits, '-' and '_'.
concepts.document: A JSON object. Its id is returned merged in under the 'id' key, so reads give one flat object rather than a wrapper.
concepts.id: 26-char sortable ULID, minted by bkn unless you supply one - pass --id, or include 'id' in the document body. Ids are immutable; patch cannot change one.
concepts.normalizer: A per-collection rule ('lower', 'upper', 'trim', 'trim_lower') declared on a field. bkn applies it on every write AND to every filter value for that field, so a lookup always finds what a write stored.
concepts.filter: A predicate on one field: field=value, field!=value, field>value, field>=value, field<value, field<=value, or field:in=a,b. Filters combine with AND. Values that parse as a number, true, false or null are compared as that type. Six operators, flat and ANDed - deliberately not a query language.
concepts.kv type: 'string' (opaque), 'json' (validated on write), or 'encrypted' (sealed with AES-256-GCM before storage, opened on read).
concepts.keyring: The set of keys that can decrypt, plus the one id that encrypts. Rotation means adding a key, pointing BKN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ID at it, and running 'bkn kv rekey'.
concepts.public entry: A kv entry marked --public is readable through the unauthenticated HTTP settings route. An encrypted entry can never be public.
concepts.script: A stored JavaScript program that must define a top-level function main(input). Its return value is the run's result. It gets store, kv and allow-listed outbound HTTP, and nothing else - no filesystem, no processes, no timers, no require.
concepts.allow_net: The per-script list of hostnames bkn.http.fetch may reach ('api.stripe.com', or '*.example.com'). Empty means no network. Connections that resolve to a private or loopback address are refused regardless, unless BKN_SCRIPT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NET=1.
concepts.run: One execution, recorded with its status (ok|error|timeout), input, result, logs and duration. Read them back with 'bkn script runs <name>'.
concepts.user: A global identity with an email (always normalized), a bcrypt password hash, and a platform role of user or admin. The platform role governs the deployment, not any tenant.
concepts.organization: A tenant, addressed by slug. Users join one through a membership that carries an org role: owner > admin > member.
concepts.access token: A short-lived (15m) HS256 JWT carrying sub, email, role, org and org_role. It cannot be revoked, which is why it is short - use 'auth me' to resolve it against the live user record.
concepts.refresh token: A long-lived (30d) opaque token, stored only as a digest and single-use: every refresh rotates it. Revocable via 'auth logout' or 'auth revoke'.
concepts.file namespace: A storage bucket with its own backend (local or s3), per-file size cap, allowed content types, and a public flag that decides whether its files are served over HTTP without auth.
concepts.content addressing: File bytes are stored under their SHA-256, never under the caller's filename. Identical uploads deduplicate, the hash is the ETag, and no user-supplied name ever reaches the filesystem.
concepts.stream: An event log namespace: 'errors', 'audit', 'cron', or whatever an app emits into. Created implicitly by the first event.
concepts.cron job: A schedule bound to a script, with optional input. Cron expressions are the usual 5 fields, plus @hourly/@daily/@weekly/@monthly/@yearly and @every <duration>.
concepts.tick: One pass over due jobs. The daemon ticks every 20s while `bkn serve` runs; `bkn cron tick` does the same pass once, for anyone driving the timing from systemd or a real crontab.
concepts.hook: A public URL (/v1/hooks/<name>) bound to a script, reachable with GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. The script receives the raw body, the lower-cased headers, the query string and the method, and returns {status, body, headers} to shape the reply - including a non-JSON Content-Type for a CSV or a feed. It MUST decide who may write: nothing else does.
concepts.lock: An expiring lease held under a key, used to stop two runs of the same work overlapping across processes. acquire returns an owner token, or null when somebody else holds it; only that owner can release or renew.
concepts.hook origin: A hook accepts cross-origin browser requests only from the origins in its allow_origin list; the preflight is refused otherwise. A provider webhook needs none, a form posted from a page needs its site listed.
concepts.ordering: store list sorts by a document field with --order-by <field> or <field>:desc, and by recency when omitted. Records missing the field sort last in both directions.
concepts.content-hash version: The version is sha256[:12] of the binary itself, so there is no number to bump: identical bytes are the same version and a rebuild that changes nothing triggers no update.
concepts.atomic_updates: A patch field may be an operator instead of a value: {"$inc":1}, {"$append":"line\n"}, {"$push":"item"}, {"$setIfEmpty":"w1"}. The new value is computed from the current one and written under compare-and-set, so concurrent patches do not lose each other's updates. A plain object is still a plain value; only a single $-prefixed key is an operator.
concepts.preconditions: store patch --if field=value and --if-absent field are checked against the document being written and are ANDed. A failed precondition writes nothing and exits 95 (precondition_failed). --if-absent claims a field exactly once, which is how one worker takes a job. There is no OR, matching the query surface.
concepts.retention: A collection may declare a bound: --retain-last N keeps the newest N documents, and --retain-per <field> gives each distinct value of that field its own N. The store enforces it on every write and when the policy is declared, so no caller writes a trim query and nothing has to be scheduled. Ordering is created_at then insertion order. No bound means unbounded; --retain-per without --retain-last is rejected because it would enforce nothing.
concepts.rollup: store count answers how many, not which. With --by <field> it returns one bucket per distinct value, largest first, alongside total (documents matching) and groups (distinct values before any limit) so truncation is visible. A document with no value for the field gets a null key, which is different from an empty string. It composes with --where, so the filter applies before the grouping. One field, one aggregate: no expressions, no having, no joins, and it never returns documents.
concepts.access policy: What a collection allows a non-admin caller to do, declared on the collection: a verb (read, create, update, delete) mapped to an audience (admin, user, owner, org, public). Undeclared means admin-only, so a collection nobody has spoken about behaves exactly as it always did. 'owner' and 'org' also scope: they need --owner-field or --org-field naming the document field that holds the user or org id, and bkn applies that as part of every read and write rather than as a check beside it.
concepts.scope stamping: On a scoped create, bkn writes the caller's own user or org id into the scope field, overwriting whatever the body said. A document cannot be created into somebody else's tenant, because the tenant is not something the client gets to state.
concepts.normalizers: A collection declares field normalization (lower, upper, trim, trim_lower). The store applies it on every write AND to every filter value for the same field, so a lookup finds the row a normalized write created. A field may name a nested key with dots, e.g. declarant.email. A path the store cannot address (array indices, quoting, wildcards) is rejected when declared rather than silently ignored.

examples.goal: Store users with an email that is always matchable regardless of how it was typed
Keep an API credential out of the environment and out of the repo
do: bkn kv set myapp.stripe_key sk_live_xxx --type encrypted --description 'Stripe live secret'

examples.goal: Rotate the encryption key without downtime
Serve the primitives over HTTP for a web app
Turn a would-be admin feature into a script
Let a script call an external API
Stand up a tenant with an owner
do: echo -n 'correct-horse-battery' | bkn auth user create ada@example.io --password-stdin --name Ada
bkn auth org create acme --name 'Acme Inc'
bkn auth member add acme ada@example.io --role owner
echo -n 'correct-horse-battery' | bkn auth login ada@example.io --password-stdin --org acme

examples.goal: Keep billing out of the user record, where it belongs
do: # a Stripe webhook handler is a script, not a core feature

examples.goal: Serve public images and keep private documents private
do: bkn files ns create avatars --backend local --allow-type 'image/*' --max-bytes 1048576 --public
curl -s localhost:7799/v1/files/avatars/ada.png -o ada.png    # no auth needed
curl -s localhost:7799/v1/files/contracts/nda.pdf             # 404 without the admin token

examples.goal: Put blobs in S3 or MinIO instead of on disk
do: bkn files ns list      # backends_available now includes s3
bkn files ns create uploads --backend s3

examples.goal: Track errors and see what is breaking most
do: bkn events emit errors http.500 --level error --source api --subject /v1/orders --data '{"trace":"abc"}'

examples.goal: Apply log retention on a schedule, with no core feature involved
do: bkn daemon start   # nothing fires without a running daemon (or `bkn cron tick`)

examples.goal: Receive a signed webhook without any core code
do: if (!bkn.crypto.equal(expected, parts.v1 || '')) return { status: 400, body: { error: 'bad signature' } };
return { status: 200, body: { ok: true, duplicate: true } };

examples.goal: Stop two runs of the same job overlapping across processes
do: bkn lock release blog-automation --force   # operator override

examples.goal: Accept a form posted from a browser, and export the results as CSV
do: bkn hooks create forms --script forms --allow-origin https://your-site.example --rate-limit 10

examples.goal: Page through a filtered, sorted collection
do: bkn store list shop/products --where 'price>20' --where status=live --order-by price:desc
# the response carries `total`, the number of matches, alongside `count`, the page size

examples.goal: Get a binary you already have onto PATH, then keep it current
do: bkn update --check    # exit 5 means an update is available
bkn update            # verifies the hash, runs the new binary, then swaps
# the previous binary is kept at <path>.bak for a manual rollback

examples.goal: Publish an update for other machines from a running bkn
do: bkn serve                       # GET /version and /dl/bkn now describe it
BKN_SERVER=https://your-host bkn update   # on the other machine

gotchas: The data file is ~/.bkn/bkn.db unless BKN_DATA says otherwise. There is exactly one resolution rule - never hardcode a path in a consumer.
patch is a shallow merge. A nested object in the patch replaces the stored one wholesale; it is not deep-merged.
store list defaults to 50 records. Pass --limit explicitly when you mean 'all', and page with --offset.
kv list never returns the value of an encrypted entry - it comes back empty. Fetch encrypted values one at a time with kv get.
Without an encryption key configured, 'kv set --type encrypted' fails loudly. It will never fall back to storing your secret in plaintext.
serve binds 127.0.0.1 by default. Binding elsewhere with --host turns on bearer-token gating for POST /_shutdown; the token is written to ~/.bkn/shutdown.token.
bkn never retries a failed operation for you. Errors carry a 'recoverable' flag and you decide.
Collections are created on first write. A typo in a namespace makes a new empty collection rather than an error - check 'bkn store collections' if a read comes back empty.

BKN_ENCRYPTION_KEY always stamps keyId 'v1' - the format the Node backend wrote. Two different single keys therefore both claim v1, and 'kv rekey' cannot tell them apart. Use BKN_ENCRYPTION_KEYS with distinct ids as soon as you have more than one key.
Ids are ULIDs and sort by creation time, including within one millisecond. Ordering by id is stable; ordering by a document field is not - store list orders by updated_at, then id.
A script must define main(input). A bare top-level expression is not the result and is never called.
There is no event loop in the script runtime: no promises, no async/await, no setTimeout. bkn.http.fetch blocks and returns its response directly.
A script with an empty allow_net has no network at all. Grant hosts explicitly, one script at a time.

Outbound requests that resolve to a loopback, link-local or private address are refused even when the hostname is allow-listed - that is what stops an allow-listed name from reaching the cloud metadata endpoint. BKN_SCRIPT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NET=1 lifts it deliberately.
Every run is bounded by timeout_ms (default 5000). The bound cannot be removed, only raised, because an unbounded script wedges the daemon.
script update only changes the flags you actually pass, so editing the code never silently resets a timeout or an allowlist.

An access token stays valid until it expires, even after a logout: revocation applies to refresh tokens. Resolve a token with 'auth me', which checks the live user record, rather than trusting its claims.
Refresh tokens are single-use. Every refresh or switch-org returns a new one and kills the old; keep the newest.
A platform admin role does NOT grant any organization role. Operating the deployment and owning a tenant are separate things.
Changing a password or disabling a user revokes that user's sessions immediately.

The token signing secret is generated on first use and kept in kv (encrypted when a keyring exists). Set BKN_AUTH_SECRET to share one across instances; rotating it invalidates every outstanding access token.
Passwords passed as --password are visible in the process table. Use --password-stdin for anything real.
Scripts are operator code, not tenant code: bkn.auth.issue can mint a session for any user. Review a script the way you would review core.

Only a short allow-list of content types is served inline (common images, text/plain, audio, video). Everything else - HTML, SVG, PDF, JavaScript - is served as an attachment with nosniff and a locked-down CSP, because serving an uploaded document inline from the API's own origin is a stored-XSS delivery mechanism.
A file in a non-public namespace is indistinguishable from one that does not exist unless you are authenticated: both answer 404.
put refuses to replace an existing name; pass --overwrite when you mean it.
Two names holding identical bytes share one blob. Deleting one keeps the other readable; the bytes go only when the last reference does.

The s3 backend appears in 'files ns list' only when S3_BUCKET, S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID and S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are set. Declaring a namespace on an unconfigured backend fails immediately rather than at the first upload.
Blobs live in ~/.bkn/files (override with BKN_FILES_DIR), separate from the database. Back up both, or neither is much use.
A script may read a file only up to 8 MB in one call; a blob store holds things a JavaScript string should not.
Cron jobs fire only while `bkn serve` is running - the scheduler lives in the daemon. Without one, use `bkn cron tick` from systemd, launchd or a real crontab; it runs exactly the same pass.

When BOTH the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted, either one matching is enough: "0 0 1 * 1" means the 1st of the month OR any Monday. That is standard cron behaviour and it surprises everyone once.
A job that is still running when its next slot arrives is skipped, not queued, and a cron.overlap warning is logged. A job slower than its interval never piles up copies of itself.
`cron run` executes immediately without consuming the scheduled slot, so testing a job does not skip its next firing.
A job whose schedule stops parsing is disabled and logged as cron.invalid rather than retried forever.
The event log has no automatic retention: it grows until something prunes it. `bkn events prune --older-than 30d` is the tool; a cron job is the usual way to run it.
Event timestamps have second resolution, so ages below a second are not meaningful.
`events stats --by` accepts only type, level, source and subject. It is the one part of the query that cannot be a bound parameter, so it comes from a fixed set.

A hook URL is PUBLIC and unauthenticated - that is the point, since providers sign requests rather than carrying a bearer token. The bound script is the only thing standing between the internet and your data: verify the signature with bkn.crypto.hmac and compare it with bkn.crypto.equal, never with ===.
A hook script that throws answers 500, so the provider retries. Return {status: 200} explicitly once you have accepted a delivery, even if you decided to ignore it.
The hook body reaches the script byte-for-byte in `body`, plus `body_base64` for payloads that are not valid UTF-8. Signatures cover exact bytes: never re-serialize before hashing.
bkn.http.fetch returns text by default and a JavaScript string is UTF-8, so binary responses are corrupted. Pass {responseEncoding:'base64'} for anything that is not text.
bkn.store.putIfAbsent returns null when the id already existed, which is the idempotency answer a webhook retry needs. A get-then-put has a race that a retry will eventually find.

A lock is a lease with an expiry, so a crashed holder cannot block the work forever - but a run that outlives its TTL loses the lock while still going. Renew it, or set the TTL above the worst-case run time.
A hook answers GET as well as POST, and the script sees d.method. An export or a form definition is fetched; a submission is posted.
A hook returning a string with a non-JSON Content-Type is written verbatim, so a CSV stays a CSV. Return an object, or set a JSON content type, and it is encoded instead.

Cross-origin browser calls are refused unless the origin is in the hook's allow_origin list - the preflight fails, so the real request never leaves the browser. A provider webhook needs no origins at all.

A public hook a browser can reach should carry --rate-limit; without one it is a spam funnel and a cheap way to fill your disk. The limit is per client IP per minute, and honours X-Forwarded-For so a proxy does not make it global.
store list returns both count (rows on this page) and total (rows matching the filter), so a paginated view can say "page 1 of 12".
Sorting is by one document field, ascending unless you write field:desc. There is no multi-field sort: if you need one, sort in a script or store a composite field.
Records that lack the sorted field sort last in both directions, rather than being buried first by SQL's NULL ordering.

Filter values are typed by how they look: price>20 compares numbers, status=true compares a boolean, name=20 compares the number 20 and not the string. Quote nothing - the store decides from the text.

Without --order-by, records come back newest first, and updated_at has second resolution: writes in the same second are ordered by id. With generated ULIDs that is still creation order; with caller-supplied ids it is alphabetical.
The id is filterable like any other field - `--where id:in=a,b,c` batch-resolves a set of references in one query instead of one get per id.
A hook receives GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE; the script branches on d.method. Only OPTIONS is handled for you, as the CORS preflight.
bkn update --check exits 5 when an update exists. That is an answer, not a failure - a shell can branch on it without parsing anything.
An update verifies the hash AND runs the downloaded binary before swapping. A truncated publish can still match its own hash, so running it is the only check that catches one.
The previous binary is kept at <path>.bak and never deleted, so a rollback is a single mv.

install COPIES the running binary rather than moving or linking it, so the file you ran it from can be deleted afterwards. It never edits your shell configuration - if the prefix is not on PATH it says so and leaves it to you.

Telemetry is opt-IN here, not opt-out: bkn holds encrypted secrets, password hashes and token signing keys, and the spec asks such tools for the stricter default. Nothing is sent until `bkn telemetry --on`.
`bkn telemetry` prints the exact payload that would be sent, and BKN_TELEMETRY_URL points it somewhere else - so what it sends can be observed without letting it send.

`bkn feedback` never fails the caller. If neither the app endpoint nor the relay is reachable it says so on stderr and still exits 0, because losing a bug report to a failed bug report is the worst outcome.
Both feedback writes carry the same id, so a retry is stored once. FEEDBACK_RELAY=off keeps submissions local.
A scoped caller reading, patching or deleting another tenant's document gets 404, not 403. Distinguishing them would confirm the id is real to somebody with no right to know that.
An access policy grants, it never revokes. Declaring read=public leaves create, update and delete admin-only, because an undeclared verb is admin.
An 'org' audience refuses a token that carries no organization rather than treating it as unscoped. Sign in with --org, or call /v1/auth/switch-org.
Cross-origin browser calls need BKN_CORS_ORIGIN set to an explicit allow-list. It is unset by default, which means no browser on another origin can call the API at all.
Self-service registration is off unless BKN_OPEN_SIGNUP=1. An open registration endpoint is a property of the deployment, not of whoever last held a token.
